 A day in the life of a poll worker during the 2026 Midterms
 By Zachary Lewis 
 ● 
 Civic Engagement 
 ● 
 November 16, 2026 
 Voters cast their vote inside the Franklin Circle Christian Church polling location in Ohio City. [Photo by Ryan Grzybowski] 
 Never have I been more exhausted than I was after working the polls Election Day. At the same time, rarely have I ever found a day of work more gratifying or more meaningful.
 I may have volunteered on a whim and even questioned my choice at times. Now, though, in retrospect, I’m perfectly clear-eyed: Signing up as a poll worker was not just the right thing to do. It was one of the best things I’ve ever done, period. 
 Initially, I almost forgot what I’d gotten myself into. I took my first step way back in February. One day, in a fit of dread over potential election interference, I visited the Ohio Board of Elections (BOE) website and registered as a poll worker. My reasoning was that if I wanted the election to run smoothly, the best thing I could do was help run it myself.
 Advertisement 
 The act induced a feeling akin to a sugar rush. There was a powerful surge of civic pride followed by a long, quiet interlude. After registering, I received no further word from the BOE until late August, when I learned my application had been accepted. 
 From there, things got real, and quickly. A few days after my acceptance email arrived, I signed up for the official poll worker training course. A few days after that , I found myself downtown at the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections, sitting in a room with about 15 fellow citizens, feeling like a kid on the first day of school.
 The training was intense. Over four packed hours, we learned how to set up, operate, and close down voting equipment; mastered eligibility requirements; and practiced checking in voters named Brad Pitt, Jennifer Aniston and Sean Penn, all of whom apparently live in Westlake but also recently moved. 
 Advertisement 
 I can’t honestly say I retained every single point that day. The instructors were great, but the information came at us like water out of a firehose. Even so, I passed the test and was comforted by assurances that I was ready. 
 Also, more training was available. I was delighted when the BOE held a review course by Zoom and a poll worker “open house,” a chance to get hands-on experience with the equipment and review setup, check-in and scanning procedures. Forget senators, governors and issues. On that day, on our fake ballots, the main subjects were our favorite superheroes.
 Fast forward to Monday night, election eve. Reporting for duty in Shaker Heights, I met my supervisors and quickly got to work setting up the location and getting to know my team, a wonderfully diverse bunch representing different ages, races and political parties. There was no political talk. However, because certain poll tasks require simultaneous participation by representatives of both parties, there was a need to know each person’s affiliation.
 The big day arrived in a flash. I went to bed early Monday night but struggled to sleep, knowing I needed to rise at 4 a.m., in time to pick up a fellow poll worker and report at 5:30. I packed enough food for two full meals. 
 The day itself was a blur, a virtually non-stop whirlwind of activity. After taking the oath of office and helping prime the equipment, I joined my team in opening the doors at 6:30 and welcoming the long line that had already formed outside the building, a queue that would grow and shrink over the course of the day but never really let up. 
 My job for the first five hours was to remind people how to submit their ballots: remove the stubs, place them in an envelope, and feed the ballot page by page into a scanner. But while I surely repeated my lines several hundred times, never was I bored. There were always stickers to hand out, pens to return, jams to clear and babies to wave at. 
 Better yet, I began encountering people I knew: neighbors, work colleagues, fellow sports parents, my pastor. It was like a wedding reception, with circles overlapping. Several people thanked me for my service. 
 My lunch break arrived – and ended – before I knew it. After scarfing a sandwich and resting my legs a moment, I felt strangely eager to jump back into the fray, and so did exactly that. This time, though, I reported to a new post, the check-in table.
 There I spent the rest of the day, minus a brief tour of duty in ballot distribution. The work suited me, and with every new issue I faced – each expired license, change of address, or soiled (mistakenly marked) ballot – I gained skills and confidence. In that way, the last seven hours flew by. 
 Our line tapered off just before the polls closed, but even at that point, at 7:30 p.m., we still had several voters filling out ballots. Only after the last person left could we begin closing down the location. 
 My job then was to help the accounting expert fill out required paperwork and share in the work of shutting down and packing up equipment. I also stepped up to help lug the heavy, sealed ballot bags out the door and into a car with our supervisors, who together drove everything back to the BOE. 
 Back home around 9:30 p.m., while I wolfed down dinner, my kids expressed amazement that I’d just worked a 16-hour day. They couldn’t imagine doing anything , let alone work, for 16 hours. They each volunteer once a month at the Greater Cleveland Food Bank, but those are two-hour shifts. 
 The results of the election pleased me greatly, but I was also gratified to see that the election itself had proceeded smoothly, without significant disruption. It wasn’t just the location where I’d worked. Nowhere had any of the scenarios I’d feared come to pass. I and all my fellow citizens across the state and nation had done their jobs well. 
 Looking ahead, after such a rewarding experience, it won’t take the threat of election interference to get me to volunteer. I’ll sign up freely. Democracy requires participation. This is something I can do.
